originalTitle: AdFection: Targeted ads turned into a pipeline for zero-click mercenary spyware
content:
This report is co-timed with an investigation by Confiant .

This section provides an overview of the online advertising ecosystem, and summarizes our findings about Discover-Tech.

The Online Advertising Ecosystem is Ripe for Abuse

When a user sees an ad on an app or a website, it is likely the result of a real-time auction, where advertisers bid on the chance to show that specific user that specific ad. So-called Real-Time Bidding (RTB) auctions, which are hosted on ad exchanges operated by companies including Google, take place hundreds of billions of times a day. In less than a second, the user’s device initiates a bid request, advertisers submit their bids, and the ad exchange determines the winner of the auction and pushes the ad to the user. Besides an image or video, an online ad can also contain code that runs within the app or browser that shows the ad.

Both advertisers and publishers of apps and websites use ad vendors that act as their intermediaries in these auctions. Advertisers typically buy ads via a so-called Demand-Side Platform (DSP), and a Supply-Side Platform (SSP) sells ad inventory on websites and apps.

Malicious actors make use of two interrelated facets of the online advertising ecosystem:

The advertising ecosystem allows many different third parties to run code in apps and websites: It is tempting to think of an online ad as, simply, a video or image. However, ads themselves may contain code from the advertiser, DSP, and other parties, and run it in the app or browser while the ad is shown to the user, for example to track users, ad impressions, and clicks. Code run by advertisers, DSPs, SSPs, and other third parties within apps and websites is often referred to as “tags”, “pixels”, “SDKs”, or “third-party tracking” more generally.

Exploiting Advertising Tech for Surveillance

The totality of information gleaned from ad auctions is quite valuable. A company with access to auction data can track users without their knowledge as they move around in physical space, or switch between cellular, Wi-Fi, and VPNs, by observing how bid requests tied to a specific identifier change location or IP address over time. In fact, the surveillance industry sells access to so-called ad intelligence (ADINT) platforms that leverage this sort of data, often combined with third-party tracking data. In recent years, several investigations and media reports have uncovered vendors that sell ADINT to defense, intelligence, and law enforcement agencies.

Beyond passive data harvesting, malicious parties can also exploit this infrastructure to target certain individuals based on user data included in ad auctions and then run malicious code on their devices. Advertisers or DSPs may run HTML and JavaScript code when an ad is shown to the user. That code retrieves additional JavaScript code, which may, in turn, load further code, such as a browser exploit to install spyware. Since the code can contain identifiers for the user or their device, arbitrary JavaScript code can be sent precisely to a single user’s device. Our research in this report indicates that this architecture is indeed abused to facilitate the delivery of zero-click targeted spyware, and that the simple display of a targeted ad is enough for infection.

Discover-Tech is a Bridge Between Mercenary Spyware Companies and the Advertising Ecosystem

We present technical evidence that the Israel-based company Discover-Tech, while purporting to be a legitimate advertising company, appears to be a front for large-scale ad espionage abuse, including the automatic delivery of mercenary spyware when ads are displayed to a target and the mass profiling and deanonymization of users.

The company serves as a bridge between ad vendors and the mercenary spyware ecosystem. In fact, it appears that serving as this bridge is Discover-Tech’s primary purpose. Its platform, Controlium, allows malicious actors to precisely profile and de-anonymize millions of individuals, fingerprint their devices, and target them with a form of zero-click hacking, where their devices can be automatically infected when an ad is displayed to them.

Discover-Tech appears to work with multiple mercenary spyware, hacking, and advertising vendors, connecting the spyware industry to the online advertising ecosystem. As we detail in this report, Discover-Tech ads are used to infect and profile on behalf of mercenary spyware vendor Candiru. We also detail connections between Discover-Tech and another mercenary hacking company, Bindecy, as well as connections with Intelos, a mercenary ADINT firm.

Discover-Tech is led by its CEO Dekel Boni, who has a background in digital advertising. Eric Banoun, whom Haaretz describes as “one of the pioneers of offensive cyber in Israel”, joined the company’s board of directors soon after it was founded in 2020 and remained there until 2025. Between 2020 and March 2026, Discover-Tech’s shareholders included a company linked to Sara Hamou, who has managed the corporate network of the spyware group Intellexa.

As detailed in Section 9 , Discover-Tech appeared on several lists of “certified” and “approved” ad vendors maintained by Google and the advertising industry association IAB Europe from the year 2020 until 2026. These listings helped make Discover-Tech appear to be a legitimate ad vendor and facilitate its participation in the digital advertising ecosystem at scale.

As a result of this investigation, both Google and IAB Europe removed Discover-Tech from their ad vendor registries in early October 2026. Google, which collaborated in the investigation, terminated Discover-Tech’s access to its ad exchange platforms.  Beeswax removed Discover-Tech from its ad buying platform, Vungle (Liftoff) paused Discover-Tech’s access while conducting a review, and Eskimi blocked Discover-Tech’s accounts and domains.
